body:
Reasoning rules, part b of 2: self-checking and problem framing (H8-H15) and verification and test design (T1-T14). TWENTY-TWO rules here, counted so a truncation is detectable; part a (reasoning-evidence-and-verification-a) holds M1-M15 and H1-H7. Consolidated from migrated memories (Greg's rules of 2026-08-23; Termal::Fable with Engram::Fable, 2026-09-07..10).

SELF-CHECKING AND ITS LIMITS
H8. Point your own review at intent (right instruction, order, addressee) and route verification of facts about artefacts outside. This is a working hypothesis, not a measured split. Why: rereading from the same position reproduces the same reading.
H9. The variable is the seat, not vigilance. Build artefacts that check themselves (announced counts, discriminating fixtures, second-party recomputation) and keep someone in the seeker's seat. Why: knowing a pattern finds it in others' work, never in your own. A small, carefully written change is exactly where the seat is missing.
H10. A success confirms the action, not the explanation. Before minting a rule from a success: (a) name the observation that would differ if the explanation were false, (b) go and look, (c) make sure the look could have come back the other way. Otherwise the rule stays a candidate.
H11. Ask why something went right while the near miss is fresh. Why: failure demands an explanation, success absorbs any story, and near misses are found only by deliberate questions.
H12. Score by whether each correction arrived before its claim could do harm, not by how many claims survived. Refuse one-sided ledgers. Why: a one-sided ledger means one side is not being checked.

PROBLEM FRAMING
H13. After the second fix that reveals a third, stop patching. First ask "what would have to be true for both symptoms to occur?" (a precondition, often answered by an inventory of states and transitions). Only then ask "can one fix cover both?" Why: if the discovery rate is not falling, you are working on symptoms.
H14. Ask "what would a third option look like?" before comparing options you were handed, and prefer stating conditions to refuting options one by one. Why: comparing consumes the attention that finding a third option needs, while a condition disqualifies variants nobody has invented yet and can move the question.
H15. When a mechanism is dismissed by reputation, check whether its precondition is guaranteed by the very situation that makes you want it (beforeunload with a non-empty draft). Why: a blanket reputation is not a check.

GREG'S RULES
T1. (Greg, reaffirmed 2026-08-23) There is no "flaky test" category. "Flaky" may describe an intermittent symptom but is never a diagnosis, excuse, quarantine or resolution. Every intermittent failure is a product bug, a badly written or synchronised test, or an invalid environment or resource assumption: remove the root cause. Never retry, quarantine, rerun until green or inflate a timeout as the fix.
T2. (Greg, 2026-08-23; current wording in CLAUDE.md "Failed gate investigation") After any build, test, typecheck or lint gate failure: stop the gated work, preserve the run and logs, investigate with focused, discriminating diagnostics, classify the cause as product, test/runner or environment/resource, and record the evidence and next action on an Engram item. Do not resume review or claim the gate passed until the original required gate succeeds. A later pass validates a fix; it does not diagnose the failure.

WRITING TESTS
T3. Assert a property that would be false under the bug, not one that is true when the feature works. Name a witness at which each assertion fails: for a bug fix, the pre-fix code; for a feature, a nearly-right variant you build; for a refactor, a variant that changes behaviour. Why: "the notice appears" is consistent with a notice that appears and is then wiped.
T4. Exercise the real path. Fixtures emit only states the real producer can reach, and test doubles perform the verb rather than record that it was requested. Why: a fixture that models ASKED as DONE cannot fail for the right reason.
T5. Pair every prohibition (safety) test or acceptance criterion with one that requires something to happen (liveness). Why: a prohibition can be satisfied by doing nothing, and a fully green suite then hides a visibly broken product.
T6. Show every check failing on a deliberately broken variant (a negative control) before its pass counts as evidence. For a guard, break the condition and show that the whole chain goes red, not merely that a message appears. Why: this proves a consumer exists, not just a signal.
T7. When a change removes or defers a behaviour, sweep every dependent test in one pass and confirm each surviving green would go red without the behaviour. Why: green is evidence about the tests as much as the product.
T8. When fixing a compile or lint error inside a test, state whether the change was type-only or behavioural, and why. Why: a quietly relaxed assertion gives a worthless green that looks real.

DESIGNING PROBES
T9. Before running a probe, name the world in which it returns the opposite result. Reject probes that cannot hit, always hit, or cannot discriminate (counting node processes to detect Vitest). Read structured fields instead of grepping the container. Detect a run by a signal that exists if and only if it started. Positive controls must share provenance with the probe. Why: a non-discriminating result travels onward as fact, and someone else's decision rests on it.
T10. Run that check hardest when the probe returns what you expected. Why: a disconfirming result triggers scrutiny on its own; a confirming one suppresses it.
T11. Ask whether the fixture on this platform actually instantiates the shape the change addresses (a process tree under a Windows .ps1 wrapper does not). Why: a green about a shape the run never contained looks like coverage, not a gap.
T12. For concurrency: to detect races, load the machine on purpose; to claim a race is absent, remove the dependence on scheduling (barriers, injected synchronisation or clock). Why: no green in any window entitles "no race", and a suite says nothing about races no test exercises.
T13. Before you run an implementer's tests, ask which ones it expects to fail and why. Why: a red for the wrong reason must be as visible as a green for the wrong reason.
T14. Ask of every control whether it would have caught the case that caused it to be written. Audit a pre-commitment ("only X is affected") before sending it. Why: a guard placed where a line was easy to add is decoration, and a false pre-commitment points attention away with settled authority.

End of part b: 22 rules (H8-H15, T1-T14).
